name: Spanish Orange
lede: Spanish Orange is a strong orange from the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, almost indistinguishable from the separately named Persimmon, and in our painting archive it shows up almost always as a highlight, not a shadow.

sections.title: A vivid orange, barely distinct from Persimmon
sections.body:
The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files this hue as a strong orange, and our library also carries it from Wikipedia's color lists; the sources we have say nothing about why "Spanish" was attached to it [1]. It is a place-or-institution name by our own classification, built on the adjective rather than any documented event [2].

Its nearest named relative, [[persimmon]], sits only 2.6 units away, close enough to call the two almost the same color under a different name [3]. A touch further off are [[safety-orange-blaze-orange]] and [[bright-orange]], both more vivid [3].

Further out again are [[bright-orange]], more vivid at 4.6 units, and [[bright-red-orange]], duller and lighter at 5.2 [3]. Unlike several of its neighbors, no Ridgway or Maerz and Paul plate reference survives for this entry in our library, only the ISCC-NBS filing and a Wikipedia source [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Spanish Orange is rare in our archive of 23,781 paintings: a color within six units of it covers at least five per cent of a canvas in just 11 works, as photographed [4]. Nearly two-thirds of its coverage in those works sits in the highlights rather than the mid-tones or shadows [4]. It is disproportionately an Indian subject: works from India carry it at nine times the archive's overall rate, and Rajput painting at over twenty-two times, including a 1745 Jaipur ragamala page where it covers nearly a fifth of the canvas [4]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors [4]. The earliest of those matches is an unidentified 1526 work attributed to Albrecht Dürer, where the color covers about 11 per cent of the canvas [4].

questions.q: Which separately named color is almost indistinguishable from Spanish Orange?
True or false: in our archive, Spanish Orange appears mostly in shadow.

openers: Spanish Orange and the separately named Persimmon are only 2.6 units apart, close to the same color.

issues: Small sample (11 archive matches) noted; no claim of strong statistical confidence beyond the counted matches.
